relations.evidence: Found a case report of severe allergic contact dermatitis caused by topical methoxypropylamino cyclohexenylidene ethoxyethylcyanoacetate; I did not find a study showing this ingredient helps acne. A review of UV filters notes acne as a discussed adverse effect for some UV filters, but not efficacy for this ingredient.

I could not identify any scientific study directly evaluating topical ethyl trimethylbenzoyl phenylphosphinate for acne. The search results retrieved acne papers unrelated to this ingredient, and no acne-specific evidence was found for this photoinitiator.

I could not find a scientific study specifically evaluating topical SACCHAROMYCES/MAGNESIUM FERMENT LYSATE FILTRATE for acne. The search returned no direct acne study on this exact ingredient. The closest retrieved paper about cosmetic postbiotics/ferments did not report acne outcomes for this ingredient specifically.
No scientific studies found linking topical aluminum hydroxy bis-methylene bis-di-t-butylphenyl phosphate to acne in the literature search performed.

relations.application: applied topically twice daily to the face
relations.evidence: A review of cosmeceuticals in acne reported that niacinamide has been studied for acne, but noted that human clinical trial evidence is limited and stronger evidence exists for other actives. One identified study in the search results is an adjunctive dermocosmetic acne study, but it does not provide direct niacinamide-only efficacy evidence.

A 2024 review of cosmeceuticals in acne vulgaris states that there is human clinical-trial evidence supporting topical retinol for acne, and a 2025 clinical study reported significant improvement in moderate-to-severe acne with a retinol plus salicylic acid topical delivery system over 12 weeks.

relations.concentration: topical retinol plus site-specific salicylic acid-targeted bio-delivery system
relations.evidence: In a 12-week study of 40 patients with moderate-to-severe acne, the retinol-containing topical system was associated with reduced inflamed pustules, fewer acne nodules, and improved post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

In 20 women with mild-to-moderate adult female acne, topical azelaic acid 15% gel used twice daily for 6 months was associated with significant clinical improvement in acne severity and erythema, along with reduced IL-6 and IL-8 expression in lesions.

A comparative split-face clinical study in 20 participants with acne vulgaris reported significant improvement in inflammatory acne lesions after 2 months of topical nicotinamide 4% cream twice daily; the study concluded nicotinamide was safe and effective, though less effective than IPL.

A clinical study of a topical retinol plus site-specific salicylic acid delivery system in 40 patients with moderate-to-severe acne reported significant improvements in inflamed pustules, acne nodules, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and Cutibacterium acnes levels over 12 weeks.

In a randomized comparative study of mild-to-moderate acne vulgaris, 30% supramolecular salicylic acid peeling was associated with decreased lesion counts over 8 weeks and showed similar observed clinical improvement to topical fusidic acid.

relations.concentration: site-specific topical salicylic acid in a retinol + salicylic acid bio-delivery system
relations.evidence: A 12-week clinical study in patients with moderate-to-severe acne reported significant improvements in lesion counts, acne nodules, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and Cutibacterium acnes levels with a retinol plus site-specific salicylic acid topical treatment.

A review on cosmeceuticals in acne vulgaris states that niacinamide is among ingredients used in acne and discusses it as an adjunctive option, but also notes that more robust human clinical trials are needed and that the strongest human evidence is for other ingredients.

A review of published clinical and experimental studies reported that there is human clinical trial evidence supporting topical retinol for acne, and another study of a retinol-containing targeted delivery system in 40 patients with moderate-to-severe acne reported significant improvements in inflammatory pustules, nodules, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and Cutibacterium acnes levels over 12 weeks.
A review on cosmeceuticals in acne vulgaris states that there is the most evidence in human clinical trials to support the use of topical retinol for acne.

A Cochrane review of topical acne treatments included 49 randomized trials and concluded that salicylic acid showed possible benefit for acne outcomes versus comparators, with low-quality evidence and no clear difference versus tretinoin in one trial. A separate review of salicylic acid as a peeling agent states that its comedolytic property makes it useful for patients with acne, and a randomized comparative study of 30% supramolecular salicylic acid peeling in mild-to-moderate acne found lesion counts decreased and clinical outcomes were similar to topical fusidic acid.

In a randomized comparative study of 30% supramolecular salicylic acid versus topical fusidic acid in mild-to-moderate acne vulgaris, lesion counts decreased in both groups over 8 weeks and salicylic acid showed similar observed clinical improvement to the comparator.

A single-arm study in moderate-to-severe acne vulgaris reported that biweekly 30% supramolecular salicylic acid peels were associated with a significant improvement in Global Acne Grading System score and skin barrier indicators after treatment.
